transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Solutions), Marta Alvarez (Nexa Head of ML), Ethan Cole (Product), Rajiv Menon (Platform), Sara Kim (Data Eng)

[00:00] Jordan: Okay we're recording, thanks everyone for joining — this is Jordan, I'm the AE, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer, and Liam on solutions — we'll run through Eval insights, show how prompt sets, regression alerts and A/B comparisons work in the console and via API.
[00:08] Marta: Great thanks, we got about an hour — heads up we have to jump at 16:00 for another sync.
[00:12] Priya: Awesome. Quick poll — has anyone used Redwood EvalOps before?
[00:18] Ethan: Not really, quick POC with a different vendor but the biggest pain was false positives on alerts and getting the thresholds right.
[00:26] Rajiv: We're mainly concerned about regressions after model upgrades and quantization changes — we don't want our shopping assistant to get more hallucinations overnight.
[00:33] Jordan: Totally, that's the typical theme. Today we'll show: (1) how to group prompts into prompt sets, (2) how to configure regression alerting and runbook links, (3) how to do an A/B compare between model variants in Console and via the API.
[00:45] Priya: I'll start share screen — bear with me if the demo gif hiccups. Uh, so this is the EvalOps console home — quick note, customers can use hosted or private — you can pin models and keep telemetry inside a VPC.
[01:02] Marta: Quick question — does the telemetry include token-level costs and per-route latency breakdown?
[01:07] Priya: Yes, we collect token usage, per-request latency, and we correlate by route, model variant and prompt set. There's a cost-per-token estimate in the dashboard, and you can export token-level traces for 30 days by default, longer with the retention add-on.
[01:22] Ethan: Can we shield PII before storing traces?
[01:25] Priya: Yes — Redwood supports field-level redaction at ingest and you can use customer KMS for encryption of logs in Private deployments. We'll send the KMS integration doc.
[01:34] [01:35] Liam: I'm going to open the "Prompt Sets" view — you can tag prompts by intent, negative examples, or include expected outputs and score functions.
[01:44] Priya: Example: here's Nexa's cart-abandonment prompt set that Marta shared earlier — we can attach evaluation metrics like BLEU (if you use), but we surface more useful quality signals for QA like response correctness (binary), policy/HL warning tags, and scalar satisfaction scores.
[02:03] Marta: We usually have around 1,200 golden prompts for checkout flows, plus 400 tricky edge cases. We want to detect when the model drops on those edge cases.
[02:12] Priya: Cool. You can set a baseline run — pick a baseline model and run the prompt set against it to get baseline metrics. Then whenever you rollout a new model the system automatically computes deltas per-metric.
[02:25] [02:27] Jordan: On alerts — you can choose absolute thresholds or relative regressions. For example we'll set an alert that triggers if the correctness rate drops by more than 3% relative to baseline over a 24-hour window.
[02:39] Ethan: How noisy are the alerts? Our SREs hate getting woken up for flakiness.
[02:43] Priya: Good point — the alerting system supports: smoothing windows, minimum sample sizes, suppression rules (by route/time), and you can wire alerts to PagerDuty, Slack, or an internal webhook that calls your runbook. There is also an automatic confidence estimate for the regression so we only alert on statistically significant drops above a configurable p-value.
[03:05] Rajiv: That p-value calculation — is it a t-test or bootstrap?
[03:09] Priya: Currently it's bootstrap-based for proportions and a Student t for continuous metrics, and we plan to expand to Bayesian approaches later — there's also a setting for minimum sample n before any alert fires.
[03:17] Marta: That helps. We're often changing prompt templates and small n effects make a difference.
[03:22] Priya: Right — that's why the prompt-set tagging and sample-size knobs matter. You can also annotate expected failure modes on a per-prompt basis so the system knows to ignore those for certain checks.
[03:33] [03:35] Jordan: Now we'll jump into an A/B comparison. Priya will trigger a split between the baseline float model and a new quantized variant to see both accuracy and latency tradeoffs.
[03:45] Priya: Running the A/B experiment now — I'm configuring a 50/50 traffic split for this prompt set, running with a 95% confidence interval and 30-minute sampling windows. The comparator will compute delta in correctness, average latency, and a composite quality score.
[04:04] Ethan: Can we compare cost too? We need to justify moving to the quantized model based on cost savings vs quality loss.
[04:09] Priya: Yes — cost per-token times tokens is shown per-arm in the experiment results, and you can set a minimum acceptable throughput/latency SLO that if violated will automatically stop a rollout.
[04:20] Marta: How does the system handle different input length distributions across arms? That could bias latency comparisons.
[04:26] Priya: Good catch — the experiment supports stratification and weighted metrics by input-length bucket. We also report median and tail latencies (p95/p99).
[04:36] [04:38] Jordan: We also have the API-first flow — if you prefer, you can push prompt sets and ground-truth labels via the API, and schedule periodic baseline runs.
[04:45] Rajiv: For the POC we'd like programmatic ingestion. Can you show the API path quickly?
[04:50] Priya: Absolutely — switching to the API quick example. You post a prompt_set JSON, then a batch evaluate endpoint accepts an array of prompts and expected outputs. Response contains per-prompt diffs and aggregate metrics. Example snippet in the quickstart: POST /v1/evalops/prompt_sets and POST /v1/evalops/batch_evaluate.
[05:08] Marta: Are there rate limits on the batch evaluate? We expect we'll evaluate tens of thousands per day in the POC.
[05:13] Priya: Not for Dedicated or Private — you can configure throughput. Hosted has default quotas which we can raise for trials. We'll include recommended batching parameters and cost estimates in the sheet.
[05:24] Ethan: We worry about data residency — some of our prompts contain customer PII. Can we keep everything inside our VPC?
[05:29] Priya: Yes, for Private you can run Redwood control plane in your VPC or on-prem. Logs and telemetry can be routed to your S3 or object store and encrypted with your KMS. We'll send the private deployment checklist.
[05:41] [05:42] Liam: Jumping back to the console, here's an example regression alert card — shows delta, p-value, sample sizes, recent failing prompts, and a quick playbook link. You can attach a runbook and a JIRA template to the alert.
[05:55] Marta: Can we auto-create tickets for top failing prompts so PMs can triage?
[05:59] Jordan: Yes, integration with Jira, linear, or internal ticketing via webhook — you can include the prompt ID, example input, and suggested rollback action.
[06:08] Ethan: Do you support automatic rollback of model rollouts?
[06:11] Priya: We support automatic safeguards — if an experiment arm violates the SLO or hits a regression threshold, it can auto-fail the rollout and revert traffic to the previous variant. That's configurable per-rollout.
[06:22] Rajiv: For our platform team the audit trail is important — do we get immutable audit logs for who changed thresholds and who ran manual evaluations?
[06:29] Priya: Yes, we log user actions, with timestamps and optional SAML SSO mapping to your identity provider. Audit logs can be exported to SIEM.
[06:36] Marta: Any visibility into model resource utilization so we can plan capacity?
[06:40] Liam: We surface per-variant throughput, GPU utilization in Dedicated, and burst capacity trends. For private, you can integrate with your monitoring stack.
[06:49] [06:50] Jordan: Let's look at an example alert that fired on a sample prompt set — Priya, can you walk through the failing prompts list?
[06:56] Priya: Sure — here's a cluster of prompts at the tail that dropped 7% in correct classification after the quantized rollout. You can click into each prompt to see original input, model outputs per-arm, scoring function evaluation and an anchor of the closest golden.
[07:13] Marta: Some of those examples are weird — I think they're edge-case templates we don't care about. Is there an ignore tag?
[07:19] Priya: Yes you can flag prompts with "ignore_for_alerts" or mark them as expected failures. You can also create a filtered alert that excludes specific tags or paths.
[07:29] Ethan: For statistical significance — how many samples do we need for a robust call?
[07:33] Priya: It depends on baseline variance — the UI will recommend a minimum sample size and show power curves. You can also run a power analysis via the API.
[07:43] Rajiv: Ok planning-wise — what's the fastest way to run a pilot?
[07:47] Jordan: Typical pilot is: share 2-3 prompt sets (1,500-3,000 prompts total), baseline run on current model, then run a 14-day A/B with the quantized variant plus a smoke alert and two playbook runbooks. We'll provision a trial workspace and temporary Elevated quotas.
[07:59] Marta: That aligns. Who needs to be involved from our side?
[08:02] Jordan: Ideally the ML lead (you), a platform contact (Rajiv) for deployment questions, and a product PM (Ethan) for success criteria and triage flow.
[08:11] [08:12] Priya: Quick note on integration — we have sample scripts to export prompt sets from your in-house test harness, and a small shim to anonymize PII before upload. We'll include that repo link in the follow-up.
[08:23] Ethan: Can we run offline baseline runs against historical traffic?
[08:26] Priya: Yes — you can upload historical inputs with ground truth to simulate rollouts and get a baseline. We also support replaying traffic to a Dedicated endpoint if you want full-stack performance testing.
[08:36] Marta: On the legal side, we need SOC2 and data processing addendum — do you have a standard DPA?
[08:40] Jordan: Yes — we'll attach SOC2 attestation and a DPA. For Private customers we do a more detailed security review and can sign a tailored DPA.
[08:49] Rajiv: Any special networking for private install? We're on AWS with strict VPC peering rules.
[08:53] Priya: We have an AWS-specific guide: VPC endpoints, cross-account IAM roles, and optional transit gateway patterns. The private install can be done with a managed control plane in your account or fully air-gapped.
[09:05] [09:06] Liam: Back to the UI — here's how you compare arms side-by-side: a waterfall view with delta bars, and you can filter by tag, by intent, or by input length. You can export a signed CSV for downstream analysis.
[09:18] Marta: Exporting will help PMs do triage in bulk.
[09:21] Priya: Exactly, and we added an "investigate" mode — it groups similar failing prompts using embedding-based clustering so you can triage clusters instead of single samples.
[09:33] Ethan: How accurate is the clustering? It sometimes groups unrelated prompts together in our experiments.
[09:38] Priya: Our clustering uses a tuned embedding model with adjustable threshold; you can set tighter or looser clustering and label clusters for later tracking.
[09:45] Jordan: Time check — we have about 15 minutes left — any remaining must-ask items?
[09:50] Marta: Two things — SLA for Dedicated customers, and whether we can get a cost model for running quantized vs float for our traffic.
[09:58] Jordan: For Dedicated we have SLAs tied to reserved capacity; we'll send the SLA doc. For cost modeling we'll run your sample distribution against both variants and return a per-day and per-1M-token estimate.
[10:10] Rajiv: Also, do you support custom metrics — we have an internal fairness score we'd like to plug in.
[10:15] Priya: Yes, you can upload custom metric hooks or client-side scoring functions; the console will ingest custom metrics and include them in experiments and alerts.
[10:24] Ethan: How do we set up alerts for multi-metric regressions? Like small drops across many metrics that are individually non-actionable.
[10:31] Priya: We have composite alerting — you can create a composite that fires when a weighted sum of metrics crosses a threshold. It's configurable from the UI and via API.
[10:40] Marta: That might be exactly what we need.
[10:43] Jordan: Last section — operationalizing. We'll recap what the pilot success looks like and next steps.
[10:47] Priya: Pilot success criteria suggestion: 1) ability to detect >3% drop on priority prompt sets, 2) integration with your Jira for automatic ticket creation, 3) cost delta report for quantized model, and 4) runbook triggers for auto-rollback.
[10:59] Marta: Works for us.
[11:01] Jordan: OK action items — we'll send the deck, an anonymization script, sandbox tenant credentials, and a sample benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:09] Ethan: One last question — are there competitor features we should know about, anything Redwood does differently?
[11:13] Priya: Compared to some vendors we combine both production-grade serving controls with EvalOps in the same platform — so experiments can fail fast and auto-roll back at the traffic layer. We also have built-in KV/prefix caching recommendations for reducing tokens and unit costs which some eval-only products don't handle.
[11:29] Marta: Great. Thanks, everybody. We should reconvene after you share the materials and after we upload our prompt sets.
[11:35] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up today with links. Recording stopped.
